critiques.summary: H1 and H2 are both grounded on verified change records (F1/F2/F13) and are temporally co-located with onset (14:00 vs 14:01, onset 14:02Z), but each rests on an unverified pivotal hop ('parser rejects a subset' / 'old-key tokens fail') and F14 explicitly states timing cannot separate them. They name DIFFERENT origins with DIFFERENT fixes (rollback deploy vs re-publish/rollback key), and the discriminating metrics — per-token-kid vs per-pod breakdown of the 401s, auth pod-level version/key-id distribution, JWKS/key-store publish timeline — were never retrieved (T1 retrieved only aggregate error_rate). This is obtainable evidence, not a permanently-down source, so the top hypothesis is not yet adequately separated from its equally-ranked rival. H3 is untested rather than contradicted (redis-cache is the only shared component; no telemetry), though T1 finding only api-gateway co-affected is a partial strike against a broad shared-component fault. Confidence cap set to reflect the H1≈H2 near-tie.

challenges.issue: The pivotal hop 'new parser rejects a subset of otherwise-valid tokens' is ASSUMED, not evidenced. The hypothesis's own assumption admits a uniform parser break would cause ~100%, not 36%, failure — and no per-token-class or per-replica breakdown exists to explain the subset. The hop is not grounded in any verified finding.

Temporal order does not discriminate: deploy (14:00) and key rotation (14:01) both precede the 14:02Z onset by 1-2 min, and F14 explicitly states the 2-min bucket resolution cannot separate them. H1 therefore does not win on timing.

The pivotal hop 'JWKS/verification path no longer resolves the old key_id' is ASSUMED. Whether k-2025-10 is still published and what fraction of in-flight tokens carry it is unknown, so the ~1/3 pattern attributed to old-key tokens is unverified.

The ~1/3-pattern-favors-key-rotation claim (F17) is a heuristic about TTL decay, not verified; a partial deploy rollout would produce the same 1/3 fraction. The two mechanisms are not separated by the observed fraction.

Untested rather than rejected: no redis-cache telemetry (hit/miss, evictions, connections) was retrieved for 14:00-14:02Z. It is only partially weakened by T1 finding no co-degradation in sibling services.
Calibration: 0.42 vs H2's 0.40 is an artificial separation of two equally-grounded candidates with unverified pivotal hops; H1 as 'top' overstates resolution.

evidence_requests.question: Break the auth-service failing 401s / error_rate down beyond the service aggregate: (a) is there any per-endpoint, per-caller, per-issuer/audience, or per-token-kid metric series available for auth-service, and if so which subset accounts for the ~36%? (b) Is there any pod/instance-level (per-replica) error_rate or version label for auth-service showing whether failures cluster on a subset of replicas vs a subset of tokens? Report exact metric names and values for 13:45-14:15Z.
evidence_requests.rationale: The single decisive discriminator between H1 (token-class/parser) and the partial-rollout reading of H1 is whether the failures cluster by token kid/audience vs by auth-service replica. Only aggregate error_rate was retrieved; this breakdown directly arbitrates H1 vs H2 and partial vs full rollout.

evidence_requests.question: Establish the fate and scope of cfg-2705: (a) is the old key k-2025-10 still published in JWKS / the key store after 14:01Z, and is there a JWKS/key-store publish or last-loaded timestamp series? (b) Was cfg-2705 scoped to a single pod/instance or the whole auth-service? (c) What token TTL/overlap/grace period is configured, and what fraction of in-flight tokens would carry k-2025-10?
evidence_requests.rationale: H2's pivotal hop (old-key tokens fail because the old key is no longer resolvable or not loaded) is unverified. If the old key is still published and resolves, H2 is contradicted and H1 becomes the clear leader; if it is not, H2 is strongly supported. This is the arbitration evidence, not mere confirmation.

evidence_requests.question: Retrieve redis-cache metrics (error_rate, connection errors, evictions, memory, hit/miss ratio) for 13:45-14:15Z, and check whether the other redis-cache consumers (portfolio-service, pricing-engine, market-data-service) show any error-rate/latency change in the same window.
evidence_requests.rationale: H3 is the only remaining distinct-origin alternative (only shared component per F3/F4/F15) and is currently untested. Co-degradation of the sibling redis consumers would support a shared fault and re-open the ranking; absence would let H3 be downgraded to a documented assumption.

critiques.summary: The two leading hypotheses (H1 dep-5710 jjwt/parser refactor at 14:00Z vs H2 cfg-2705 signing-key rotation at 14:01Z) are both well-grounded on verified change records and both remain temporally co-located with the 14:02Z onset (F14 shows timing cannot separate them). Round 2 resolved the *obtainable* questions: H3 (shared redis-cache) is now properly tested and contradicted (F25-F29: cache metrics flat, all three sibling consumers flat ~0.2%), and api-gateway is ruled out (F16/F35). But the decisive discriminators between H1 and H2 are demonstrated by T4/T5 to be permanently unavailable for this incident, not merely unqueried: auth-service exposes no per-kid/issuer/audience or per-replica/version metric, logs are unretrievable (503), and no tool exposes JWKS/key-store publish state, key last-loaded series, or token TTL/overlap/grace config, nor is a key-store node present in the dependency graph (F21, F23). Each hypothesis still rests on exactly one unverified pivotal hop (H1: 'parser rejects a subset'; H2: 'old key no longer resolves'). They name different origins with different fixes (roll back the deploy vs re-publish/roll back the key), and no further query in the available tool surface would separate them. Therefore the outcome is inconclusive rather than accept or needs_evidence. The team should note that the triggers are firmly localized to auth-service (one of its two 14:00-14:01Z changes), but which one cannot be determined from retrievable data; the ~1/3-vs-36% 'matches a token-TTL population' claim for H2 is an unverified quantitative fit (no TTL value exists), and H1's 'rejects only a subset, not all' mechanism is likewise assumed, with the flat 36% mildly against a uniform parser break.

challenges.issue: Pivotal hop 'the rewritten jjwt 0.12 parser rejects a subset (~36%) of otherwise-valid tokens rather than all' is ASSUMED and untested; a uniform parser/claim-parsing break would be expected to yield ~100% failure, so the flat 36% step is mildly inconsistent with the stated mechanism, yet H1 remains co-ranked first.

Partial-rollout reading (failures on a subset of replicas) cannot be tested: no per-replica/version metric and restarts flat at 0 (F31, F32). The 'subset' is therefore unattributed between token-class and replica-class, so H1's mechanism variant is unverified either way.

Pivotal hop 'verification path no longer resolves old key k-2025-10' is neither supported nor refuted: no JWKS publish state, key last-loaded series, or key-store node exists (F21, F22, F23). H2 rests entirely on a lead incident (HIST-108), not current evidence.

The quantitative fit to the ~1/3 failure share is asserted with no measurement: no token TTL/overlap/grace config and no issuance-by-kid distribution are retrievable (F20, F23), so whether old-key tokens could even account for ~36% of validations for 2h un-decayed is unverified.

Now contradicted rather than merely untested: cache metrics flat across onset and all three sibling redis-cache consumers flat at ~0.2% (F25-F29). Residual uncertainty only — redis-cache cpu/memory for the onset window were requested but budget-exhausted, though hit ratio/clients/evictions already cover health.
Correctly rejected, but its supporting evidence (F11) is the same gateway 5xx that also merely reflects an auth-calling subset; the rejection is sound and not blocking.
